title: Multimodal Breast MRI Language-Image Pretraining (MLIP): An Exploration of a Breast MRI Foundation Model
reason_for_exclusion: Useful early breast-MRI foundation-model experiment, but the output is still mainly retrieval and BI-RADS-style inference. liu2025bootstrapping and sanli2025interpreting fit the review better for MRI report interpretation, while chen2025sam2med3d is closer to planning-oriented MRI segmentation.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles the lack of structured annotations and breast-MRI-specific foundation models by learning joint representations from breast MRI volumes and paired radiology reports. The goal was to build MLIP, a multimodal language-image pretraining model that supports clinically relevant MRI retrieval and downstream BI-RADS prediction. Its novelty is a CLIP-style framework adapted to 3D breast MRI, using a 3D ResNet50 image encoder and a radiology-specific RadioLOGIC text encoder; the authors position it as an initial exploration of a breast MRI foundation model. The main takeaway from the full-text results is that the approach is feasible and promising for suspicious-case retrieval, but performance for density/BPE retrieval and BI-RADS agreement is still modest, indicating the need for larger multi-center data, cleaner supervision, and more region-focused modeling.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Netherlands Cancer Institute (NKI) breast MRI-report cohort (private, single-center): training set of 15,005 paired cases; validation set of 3,013 unprocessed / 1,704 processed pairs; test set of 738 unprocessed / 380 processed pairs for BI-RADS analyses; density test subset of 100 pairs; low-BPE test subset of 155 pairs
Baseline model/architecture: MLIP (proposed CLIP-style multimodal model; no separate external baseline reported): 3D ResNet50 image encoder + RadioLOGIC text encoder + separate projection heads mapped to a shared 256-dimensional embedding space; downstream evaluation used the pretrained model in zero-shot form and a fine-tuned version for BI-RADS prediction
Training Approach: Weakly supervised multimodal contrastive language-image pretraining on paired MRI-report data with bidirectional image-to-text and text-to-image loss; all parameters trainable; AdamW optimizer; 20 epochs; batch size=4; followed by zero-shot BI-RADS prediction and additional downstream fine-tuning for BI-RADS classification
Medical Modality: Breast DCE-MRI, including pre-contrast and subtraction images
Model input modality: image+text during pretraining (3D MRI volumes + radiology reports); image + text queries/prompts during retrieval and BI-RADS inference
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: BI-RADS 4/5 retrieval: AUC=0.717 (95% CI 0.604-0.824), Sensitivity=0.500, Specificity=0.868 at similarity threshold 0.433; Dense-breast retrieval: AUC=0.640 (95% CI 0.538-0.740), Sensitivity=0.327, Specificity=0.938 at threshold 0.435; Low-BPE retrieval: AUC=0.601 (95% CI 0.505-0.698), Sensitivity=0.518, Specificity=0.667 at threshold 0.354; BI-RADS human-AI agreement: Gwet's AC1=0.18 (95% CI 0.10-0.26) for zero-shot and 0.23 (95% CI 0.15-0.30) after fine-tuning

title: MedFocusCLIP : Improving few shot classification in medical datasets using pixel wise attention
reason_for_exclusion: Too general for this manuscript. It is a few-shot medical-image classification method across datasets, while the review already has more breast-relevant few-shot and VLM examples through wang2025pm2 and ghosh2024mammo.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the challenge of few-shot medical image classification, where standard CLIP-style prompting can miss subtle disease-specific cues and offers limited interpretability. The main goal is to improve low-data classification by guiding the model toward clinically relevant regions of interest. The novelty is MedFocusCLIP, which uses zero-shot SAM2 segmentation masks as pixel-wise visual prompts before CLIP encoding, then combines image and text representations for classification. Unlike prior work that depends more heavily on supervised fine-tuning or manual/domain-specific prompt design, the method uses SAM2-derived localization to focus attention without supervised segmentation labels. The main takeaway is that ROI-guided CLIP consistently improves performance over CLIP, CoOp, CoCoOp, and standard CNN/Transformer baselines across several medical imaging datasets, especially in few-shot settings.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: COVID-19 dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated); Lung Disease dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated); Brain Tumor dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated); Breast Cancer dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated)
Baseline model/architecture: MedFocusCLIP = SAM2-generated segmentation mask + CLIP image encoder (ViT backbone) + CLIP text encoder + multimodal fusion + classification head / linear probe; main comparators: CLIP, CoOp, CoCoOp, ResNet, Res2Net, ViT, Swin Transformer; ablations: SAM Adapter in place of SAM2, and Swin Transformer in place of CLIP
Training Approach: Few-shot supervised classification; SAM2 is used in zero-shot/inference mode to generate ROI masks; masked images and text prompts are processed by CLIP; the paper describes a composite loss L = λLc + (1−λ)Le (contrastive + cross-entropy); evaluation is performed with linear probing using logistic regression on frozen multimodal embeddings
Medical Modality: Multi-modal medical imaging (explicitly stated: X-ray, CT, MRI; exact modality-to-dataset mapping is not fully specified in the paper)
Model input modality: Image + text (medical image after SAM2 masking/segmentation + class-name or descriptive text prompt)

title: A clinical benchmark of public self-supervised pathology foundation models
reason_for_exclusion: Mainly a benchmark of public pathology encoders across health systems. Useful background, but it would not add much to the breast-surgery narrative beyond what lee2025benchmarking and kim2025predicting already provide.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper benchmarks public self-supervised pathology foundation models on 22 clinically relevant slide-level tasks from three real-world health systems. The goal is to identify which public encoders generalize best to routine clinical pathology data and to understand what pretraining factors matter for downstream performance. The novelty is a multi-institutional benchmark built from standard hospital workflow data, a standardized frozen-encoder plus GMA evaluation pipeline, and analyses of model size, pretraining dataset size/composition, and inference cost. The main takeaway is that DINO/DINOv2-based pathology encoders outperform ImageNet and usually outperform CTransPath, but bigger models or bigger pretraining sets do not guarantee better results; dataset composition appears more important, especially for biomarker tasks.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Benchmark/evaluation datasets (all private/internal; benchmark data not publicly released): MSHS Breast Cancer Detection; MSHS Oral Cancer Detection; MSHS Bladder Cancer Detection; MSHS Kidney Cancer Detection; MSHS Thyroid Cancer Detection; MSHS DCIS Detection; MSHS Prostate Cancer Detection; MSHS Colo-rectal Cancer Detection; MSHS IBD Detection; MSHS Breast ER; MSHS Breast PR; MSHS Breast HER2; MSHS BioMe HRD; SUH Melanoma BRAF; SUH Melanoma NRAS; MSHS LUAD EGFR; MSKCC LUAD EGFR; MSKCC LUAD ALK; MSKCC LUAD STK11; MSKCC LUAD KRAS; MSKCC LUAD TP53; MSKCC NSCLC ICI response. Additional in-house pretraining dataset for SP22M/SP85M: MSHS 423,563 H&E slides (private).
Baseline model/architecture: Frozen tile-level pathology foundation encoders evaluated with a Gated MIL Attention (GMA) slide aggregator and linear classifier. Key encoders: UNI, Virchow, Prov-GigaPath, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, Phikon, Phikon-v2, CTransPath, plus in-house DINO ViT-small SP22M and DINO ViT-base SP85M; comparator baseline: ImageNet-pretrained truncated ResNet-50 (tRes50).
Training Approach: Self-supervised pretrained tile encoders (mostly DINO/DINOv2; also iBOT and SRCL for some models) were kept frozen, and downstream tasks were trained in a supervised slide-level MIL setup. Tissue tiles were extracted at 20x, embedded by each encoder, and aggregated with GMA. Evaluation used 20 Monte Carlo cross-validation splits with 80/20 train-validation sampling, two replicas per split, 50 epochs, AdamW, and cosine decay with warm-up.
Medical Modality: Digital histopathology whole-slide images, primarily H&E WSIs at 20x; downstream labels came from pathology diagnosis, IHC/FISH, NGS, BioMe genetics, and RECIST-based ICI response
Model input modality: Image-only (H&E tile images / slide embeddings; no text or tabular input to the model)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: validation AUC across 20 MCCV splits. Detection tasks: all models achieved AUC > 0.90; average detection AUC examples reported in the paper were H-optimus-0 = 0.980 and SP85M = 0.978. Biomarker tasks: average biomarker AUC examples were H-optimus-0 = 0.785 and UNI = 0.773. NSCLC ICI response was difficult, with UNI average AUC = 0.60 and other models near chance. Scaling analyses: model size vs downstream performance Pearson r = 0.055 (detection, p = 2.59e-2) and r = 0.091 (biomarker, p = 9.52e-6); pretraining dataset size showed weak/no strong correlation with downstream AUC.

title: Tissue concepts: Supervised foundation models in computational pathology
reason_for_exclusion: Broad supervised pathology encoder, not a breast-planning application. lee2025benchmarking and zhao2024aligning already cover pathology foundation models with a closer link to the review.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper addresses whether supervised multi-task learning can produce a pathology foundation model without the data and compute burden of large self-supervised pretraining. It proposes Tissue Concepts, a shared histopathology encoder trained jointly on 16 classification, segmentation, and detection tasks from diverse annotated datasets, then evaluates frozen features via multiple-instance learning on breast, prostate, colorectal, and lung whole-slide image classification with cross-center testing. The main novelty is replacing massive unlabeled pretraining with supervised multi-task pretraining on about 912,157 patches while still learning transferable tissue representations. The main takeaway is that Tissue Concepts is broadly comparable to self-supervised pathology encoders such as CTransPath and clearly stronger than ImageNet features, although out-of-domain lung performance remains weaker than models pretrained directly on lung-rich datasets.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Pretraining (all public): NCT-CRC-HE-100K (public); CRAG (public); SemiCOL segmentation subset (public); CoNIC (public); Arvaniti TMA (public); PESO (public); Schoemig-Markiefka prostate dataset (public); PANDA (public); TUH breast subset (public); TIGER (public); BCSS (public); BreakHis (public); MIDOG 2022, excluding lung cases in pretraining (public); HuBMAP large-intestine subset (public). Ablation: BACH (public). Downstream validation: BRACS (public); PANDA (public); SemiCOL WSI set (public); TCGA-NSCLC = TCGA-LUAD + TCGA-LUSC (public).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: Tissue Concepts encoder with Tiny Swin Transformer backbone (TC-Swin; 27.5M params, 768-d latent); also a Tiny ConvNeXt variant (TC-Conv). Pretraining uses a shared U-Net-style decoder for segmentation and an FCOS detection head; downstream whole-slide classification uses a small CNN MIL head over latent WSIs. Main baselines/comparators: CTransPath, ImageNet-pretrained tiny Swin, UMedPT (ablation), plus published external baselines such as HACT-Net for BRACS, Mahdi Behzadi et al. for PANDA, and TransMIL/CTransPath literature baselines for lung.
Training Approach: Supervised multi-task learning across 16 tasks from 14 histopathology data sources, spanning classification, segmentation, and detection; ImageNet-1k initialization; 224x224 patches with standard augmentation. Pretraining used AdamW (lr=1e-4, weight decay=0.01, gradient accumulation=128) for 5 million task-steps, taking about 160 hours on one NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU. Downstream evaluation froze the encoder and trained slide-level multiple-instance learning classifiers on latent whole-slide representations; an ABMIL alternative was tested in the appendix.
Medical Modality: Histopathology / computational pathology; H&E-stained whole-slide images and extracted tissue patches, with some segmentation masks and detection annotations.
Model input modality: Image-only during pretraining (224x224 histopathology patches); downstream MIL head receives image-derived latent whole-slide feature maps only; no text or tabular clinical input.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: BRACS: 2-class wF1=0.951 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.992 +/- 0.001; 4-class wF1=0.545 +/- 0.04, AUC=0.830 +/- 0.01; 7-class wF1=0.405 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.769 +/- 0.02 (TC-Swin). PANDA: 5-fold Acc=0.942 +/- 0.01, F1=0.928 +/- 0.01, AUC=0.983 +/- 0.01 (TC-Swin), with best overall 5-fold TC-Conv Acc=0.957 +/- 0.05, F1=0.947 +/- 0.06, AUC=0.990 +/- 0.01; Karolinska to Radboud TC-Swin Acc=0.896 +/- 0.01, F1=0.829 +/- 0.01, AUC=0.914 +/- 0.02; Radboud to Karolinska TC-Swin Acc=0.846 +/- 0.02, F1=0.842 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.926 +/- 0.01. SemiCOL average cross-center: Acc=0.953 +/- 0.02, F1=0.953 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.989 +/- 0.01 (TC-Swin). TCGA-NSCLC: 5-fold Acc=0.878 +/- 0.02, F1=0.875 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.949 +/- 0.01; cross-center Acc=0.785 +/- 0.01, F1=0.778 +/- 0.01, AUC=0.863 +/- 0.01 (TC-Swin). Ablation/BACH sample efficiency: mean F1=0.816 for TC-Swin with maximum training images/class vs 0.762 for UMedPT and 0.662 for ImageNet.

title: When multiple instance learning meets foundation models: Advancing histological whole slide image analysis
reason_for_exclusion: Another WSI foundation-model and MIL benchmark. Methodologically relevant, but too far from the manuscript's clinical workflow; lee2025benchmarking and kim2025predicting are enough for this part.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This is a full-text benchmark study of weakly supervised computational pathology rather than a generative-AI or surgical-planning paper. It addresses the lack of unbiased evidence on how histology-specific foundation models compare with multiple-instance-learning (MIL) aggregators for whole-slide image classification. The authors systematically benchmark six patch encoders and six slide-level MIL aggregators across seven clinical tasks spanning breast, glioma, liver, and colorectal cancer using 4044 patients from public and private multi-center cohorts. Its main novelty is the broad, controlled comparison across binary, multi-class, and multi-label tasks with both internal cross-validation and external testing. The main takeaway is that domain-specific foundation models, especially UNI and CONCH, generally outperform ImageNet ResNet50 and often other pathology FMs, while online feature re-embedding aggregators such as RRT can further help and stronger encoders also reduce convergence time.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: QHSU breast cohort (private); SHSU breast cohort (private); QCH breast cohort (private); TCGA Glioma (public); SAHDMU Glioma cohort (private); GPPH Liver cohort (private); TCGA-CRC cohort (public)
Baseline model/architecture: Patch encoders compared: UNI (ViT, DINOv2), CONCH (ViT visual-language FM, CoCa), CTransPath (CNN+Swin hybrid), PathoDuet (ViT), PLIP (CLIP-based visual-language model), and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 baseline; slide-level MIL aggregators: ABMIL, CLAM-MB, DTFD, TransMIL, RRT, WiKG
Training Approach: Weakly supervised embedding-based MIL with slide-level labels only; 256x256 non-overlapping 20x H&E patches extracted after CLAM-style tissue detection; pretrained encoders used for offline patch embeddings, with some aggregators performing online feature re-embedding (especially TransMIL, RRT, WiKG); patient-level 5-fold cross-validation plus external cohort testing where available; AdamW, learning rate=1e-4, batch size=1, max 100 epochs, early stopping on validation AUROC; cross-entropy for multi-class tasks and masked multi-label binary cross-entropy for ER/PR/HER2
Medical Modality: Histopathology whole-slide imaging; H&E-stained digital pathology WSIs
Model input modality: image-only (bags of WSI patches / patch embeddings)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Reported as mean ± SD, mainly AUROC and AUPRC. Best task-wise results: Breast grading—QHSU AUROC=86.07±2.47%, AUPRC=70.81±5.45% (UNI+RRT); SHSU AUROC=91.98±1.01% (PathoDuet+DTFD), AUPRC=90.29±0.75% (CTransPath+CLAM-MB); QCH AUROC=92.57±0.53% (UNI+DTFD), AUPRC=85.02±1.70% (CTransPath+CLAM-MB). QHSU biomarkers—ER AUROC=93.09±1.87%, AUPRC=97.47±0.97% (UNI+RRT); PR AUROC=87.01±1.41% (UNI+RRT), AUPRC=93.98±0.65% (UNI+CLAM-MB); HER2 AUROC=90.69±1.02%, AUPRC=80.74±1.77% (UNI+DTFD). SHSU biomarkers—ER AUROC=91.64±0.81% (UNI+ABMIL), AUPRC=97.82±0.26/0.52% tie (UNI+CLAM-MB or UNI+RRT); PR AUROC=86.86±0.86%, AUPRC=96.16±0.29% (UNI+WiKG); HER2 AUROC=85.77±2.75% (PLIP+CLAM-MB), AUPRC=76.07±2.40% (CTransPath+CLAM-MB). Glioma grading—TCGA AUROC=91.77±1.84%, AUPRC=80.74±5.08% (CONCH+CLAM-MB); SAHDMU AUROC=91.51±0.91%, AUPRC=78.17±2.53% (CONCH+CLAM-MB). Liver grading—AUROC=75.96±1.13% (UNI+ABMIL), AUPRC=49.37±3.48% (UNI+DTFD). CRC MSI—AUROC=86.95±4.90% (UNI+RRT), AUPRC=63.15±17.62% (CONCH+ABMIL).

title: Improved Osteoporosis Prediction in Breast Cancer Patients Using a Novel Semi-Foundational Model
reason_for_exclusion: Osteoporosis screening in breast-cancer patients is a side issue here, not breast tumor assessment or surgery planning. Survivorship and outcome extraction are already better handled by luo2024automated and zhu2025large.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses opportunistic osteoporosis / bone demineralization prediction in breast cancer patients younger than 65 using routine staging CT, where labeled cohorts are small and DEXA screening is not routinely available. The goal was to test whether a semi-foundational model pretrained on an unrelated but CT-native dataset could improve downstream 3-class L1 vertebral demineralization classification. The main novelty is not generative AI, but modality-specific pretraining on external COVID-19 chest CT before fine-tuning on a small breast-cancer cohort, with comparison against random initialization and ImageNet-only transfer. The full-text discussion also highlights that Grad-CAM attention concentrated on pedicles / cortical bone rather than the usual medullary ROI, suggesting a potentially different imaging biomarker strategy. The main takeaway is that CT-native pretraining substantially improved performance, with semi-foundational ResNet50 achieving near-perfect holdout results in this cohort.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: COVID-19 Lung CT database, 8,439 chest CT scans (public); USF Health retrospective breast cancer cohort from initial staging PET-CT, CT component only, 199 eligible patients from 866 screened (private)
Baseline model/architecture: Semi-foundational CNNs: ResNet50 (best), VGG16, DenseNet121; comparator transfer settings were random / no transfer, ImageNet initialization, and COVID-19 CT-pretrained weights
Training Approach: Supervised transfer learning / fine-tuning; base CNNs initialized from ImageNet, pretrained on COVID-19 chest CT binary classification, then fine-tuned for 3-class osteoporosis / demineralization classification on L1 CT slices; 5-fold cross-validation on 160 patients, 20% holdout test (n=40), SMOTE class balancing, hyperparameter tuning with Keras Tuner plus manual tuning, Adam optimizer with categorical cross-entropy
Medical Modality: CT (non-contrast CT component of PET-CT; single axial L1 vertebral bone-window slice)
Model input modality: image-only (2D single-slice CT PNG)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Best model = semi-foundational ResNet50 with COVID-19 CT pretraining: Validation AUC=0.95 (95% CI 0.88-1.00); Holdout Accuracy=0.99; Testing AUC=0.99; F1-score=0.99; Precision=0.99; Recall=0.99

title: Exploring Patient Data Requirements in Training Effective AI Models for MRI-Based Breast Cancer Classification
reason_for_exclusion: The main question is how much MRI data is needed to train a classifier. Useful, but mostly a data-sufficiency study; chen2025sam2med3d and gao2025multi are closer to planning because they deal with tumor segmentation and treatment-response prediction.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper asks a practical deployment question for MRI-based breast cancer classification: how much local patient data is needed to train a competitive AI model. Using the full Duke cohort, the authors created 80 patient-level training sets of different sizes and compared ViT-B/16 models initialized with DINO, MAE, supervised ImageNet pretraining, or random weights. The novelty is a data-sufficiency analysis rather than a new classifier: it quantifies diminishing returns, checks whether patient selection matters, and tests a simple ensemble. The main takeaway is that transfer learning from foundation models, including a generative-pretrained MAE model, can achieve competitive performance with surprisingly small cohorts, and performance differences across training splits become small once about 50 patients are used. A simple majority-vote ensemble further improves results with minimal added complexity.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Duke Breast Cancer Dataset (public; 922 patients; main downstream dataset; 3D breast MRI converted to 2D slices); ImageNet (public; source of pretrained weights for DINO, MAE, and supervised ViT models); no external validation cohort reported
Baseline model/architecture: Vision Transformer Base/16 (ViT-B/16); compared variants: DINO-pretrained ViT-B/16, MAE-pretrained ViT-B/16, supervised ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16, randomly initialized ViT-B/16; simple majority-vote ensemble of the three pretrained models
Training Approach: Transfer learning/fine-tuning of ImageNet-pretrained foundation models plus a from-scratch comparator; supervised binary classification with cross-entropy on 224x224 2D MRI slices; patient-level stratified sampling with n={1,5,10,50,100,200,400,700} patients and 10 splits each, plus a fixed 200-patient validation set; SGD grid search (lr=0.1/0.01/0.001, weight decay=0 or 0.0001, momentum=0 or 0.1), cosine annealing, random resized crop augmentation, early stopping; inference-time majority-vote ensemble
Medical Modality: Breast MRI (3D MRI volumes converted to 2D slices)
Model input modality: Image-only (single 2D MRI slices, 224x224)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Validation metrics reported: Accuracy, F1-score, and Precision. Best exact tabulated 50-patient ensemble results across 10 splits: Accuracy=0.770 (split 6) and F1=0.797 (split 4); the ensemble outperformed the best individual model in accuracy in 9/10 splits. Best exact individual-model values in the same table: DINO Accuracy=0.763 and F1=0.788; MAE Accuracy=0.770 and F1=0.791; Supervised Accuracy=0.755 and F1=0.775. Precision was also analyzed across patient counts/splits in boxplots, but the paper did not fully tabulate those numeric values.

title: Simulation training in mammography with AI-generated images: a multireader study
reason_for_exclusion: Radiology-training simulator, not a surgical-planning tool. It does not support breast surgery decisions, so the space is better used for planning-relevant mammography work such as cao2025mammovlm and ghosh2024mammo.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addressed the lack of flexible, high-variety training material for learning mammographic cancer detection. The main goal was to build a controllable generative-AI simulator that can create realistic mammograms with adjustable breast characteristics and allow cancer insertion for practice. Its novelty was not just synthetic image generation, but combining an adversarial latent autoencoder with PCA-based latent controls, Poisson blending for realistic lesion insertion, and a web interface that was then tested in a randomized multireader educational study. The main takeaway is that this simulator improved resident mammogram-reading performance, especially among junior trainees, showing value for breast-imaging education rather than direct surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Retrospectively collected anonymized patient mammogram images used to train the model (private/internal; exact cohort name and size not reported in the main text); fidelity reader-study set: 50 real mammograms (private/internal) + 50 GAN-generated mammograms (synthetic/internal); resident performance test set: 100 mammograms (private/internal; 38 negative and 62 biopsy-proven cancers).
Baseline model/architecture: ALAE (Adversarial Latent Autoencoder; GAN-family architecture) with encoder-generator-discriminator framework; PCA over latent vectors for controllable mammographic feature editing; Poisson blending for lesion insertion; no conventional ML baseline reported, and the main comparator was a non-practice resident control arm.
Training Approach: Ambispective design: retrospective internal mammograms were used for unsupervised/generative adversarial training of the ALAE; PCA-based latent-space manipulation was used at inference to control density, size, and tissue distribution; cancers were added via user-guided segmentation plus Poisson blending; the educational effect was evaluated prospectively in a randomized multireader study.
Medical Modality: Mammography (breast X-ray)
Model input modality: Image-only mammograms; in the simulator, an uploaded normal mammogram is the main input, with an optional second abnormal mammogram / segmented lesion used for blending.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Resident-performance endpoint in practice group (Test 1 to Test 2): Sensitivity 50.51% to 57.94% (+7.43 percentage points; within-group p=0.015; vs non-practice p=0.030); Specificity 70.35% to 75.30% (+4.95 pp; within-group p=0.264; vs non-practice p=0.661); PPV 76.82% to 82.40% (+5.58 pp; within-group p=0.058; vs non-practice p=0.454); NPV 42.23% to 47.28% (+5.05 pp; within-group p=0.002; vs non-practice p=0.008); Accuracy 57.25% to 63.74% (+6.49 pp; within-group p=0.001; vs non-practice p=0.010). Fidelity test of realism: expert readers distinguishing real vs generated mammograms achieved 48% accuracy (Reader 1) and 45% accuracy (Reader 2).

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Synthesizing High-Fidelity Breast Thermal Images
reason_for_exclusion: Thermal-image synthesis is too far from the breast-surgery workflow used in the manuscript. It also stays at synthetic image quality, while raheem2025fame and alhussan2025fed are more useful examples of synthetic data for breast imaging.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the shortage of large, high-quality breast thermography datasets by testing whether generative AI can synthesize realistic breast thermal images. The main goal was to compare three generative families - DCVAE, DCGAN, and DDPM - and identify which one best produces high-fidelity synthetic thermograms. Its novelty is the direct benchmarking of VAE-, GAN-, and diffusion-based image synthesis specifically for breast thermal imaging on a very large real-world cohort, an area with little prior published work. The study found that DDPM generated images that most closely matched the real data distribution and clearly outperformed DCGAN and DCVAE on fidelity. This is best viewed as an upstream data-generation study for breast-screening/diagnostic AI rather than a direct surgical-planning model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Unnamed internal multi-center breast thermography cohort from multiple hospitals, clinics, and outreach camps; 102,459 participants; 5 standard views per participant (private). No public dataset or external validation dataset was reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Compared models: DDPM with a 4-stage U-Net denoiser; DCGAN with a 4-block transpose-convolution generator and a VGG-based discriminator; DCVAE with a deep convolutional encoder-decoder and latent dimension 256.
Training Approach: Unsupervised generative modeling trained from scratch on min-max normalized 240x320 thermal images using Adam. Minimal data augmentation included Gaussian noise addition, random flipping, rotation, and cropping. DCVAE used a VAE reconstruction + KL objective, DCGAN used adversarial min-max training, and DDPM used weighted-MSE denoising diffusion training with 1000 timesteps. All models were randomly initialized; DDPM additionally used gradient accumulation of 4.
Medical Modality: Breast thermography / infrared thermal imaging; multi-view 2D FLIR thermal camera images
Model input modality: image-only during training (2D thermal images); random noise/latent sampling for image generation
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: FID (Inception-v3 feature based). DDPM=18.065; DCGAN=129.714; DCVAE=150.848. Reference real-vs-real FID=0.47. Additional reported comparison values: inference time - DDPM=12 s, DCGAN=78 ms, DCVAE=18 ms; trainable parameters - DDPM=9,196,161, DCGAN=30,128,769, DCVAE=20,464,977.

title: Ionic Cell Microscopy: A new modality for visualizing cells using microfluidic impedance cytometry and generative artificial intelligence
reason_for_exclusion: Clever cell-imaging proof of concept, but not a patient-level breast cancer planning study. The review already covers more clinically meaningful visual-biological links through chen2025visual and farooq2023understanding.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper addresses label-free visualization of cells without relying on conventional optical microscopy by reconstructing cell images from electrical impedance signals acquired in a custom microfluidic chip. Its main goal is to convert single-cell impedance responses into 51 x 51 pixel images for 5 um beads, HeLa cells, and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. The novelty is that it uses what the authors call 'Ionic Cell Microscopy' - a generative AI workflow that maps a 191-value impedance vector directly to an image, going beyond standard impedance-based classification. The main takeaway is that this proof-of-concept produced high-fidelity reconstructions, especially for breast cancer cells and beads, suggesting a portable, label-free imaging approach, although broader validation on more cell types and larger datasets is still needed.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal Rutgers experimental dataset of paired impedance signals and reference high-speed microscopy images for 5 um beads, HeLa cells, and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells (private; data available on request). No public dataset or external validation cohort reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Custom fully connected generative DNN / MLP; input layer = 191 nodes; 8 hidden layers = 100, 80, 40, 50, 30, 15, 20, 1000; output layer = 2601 nodes reshaped to a 51 x 51 image. No explicit external baseline comparator reported.
